title: Vidagdha Shakalya: how many gods? 3,306 → 33 → 6 → 3 → 2 → 1½ → 1 (3.9)
hook: the last challenger asks how many gods there are, and keeps asking until the number counts down to one

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gargi's two arrows drew out akshara, the imperishable, without inside or outside. Your line was neither coarse nor fine.

People sometimes say Hindus have three hundred thirty million gods. The Upanishad has its own count, and it's a countdown. The last challenger, Vidagdha Shakalya, asks Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, he answers. Yes, says Shakalya. But how many gods are there, really? Thirty-three. Yes, but how many really? Six. Really? Three. Really? Two. Really? One and a half. And how many gods are there, really? One.

Then Shakalya makes him explain each number. The three thousand and more, Yajnavalkya says, are only their powers. There are really thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, and Indra and Prajapati. The Vasus are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, sun, sky, moon and stars: everything dwells in them. The Rudras are the ten breaths in a person, and the self: when they leave the body, they make people weep. The Adityas are the twelve months, carrying everything along. Indra is the thunder; Prajapati is the sacrifice. The six are fire, earth, wind, the middle air, the sun and the sky. The three are the three worlds. The two are food and breath. The one and a half? The wind that blows, because everything grows in it. It's a pun in Sanskrit; it doesn't translate. And the one? Breath. It is Brahman. They call it That. Notice what didn't happen: the countdown never says the many gods were a mistake. They fold onto one, like a fan folding shut. A verse in the Rig Veda says it in a single line: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Hindus live this in different ways. Some worship one form of God as supreme, and see the others as that God's forms or helpers. Others honor many deities, each in its place. Advaita teachers hear in the count one reality appearing as many. This passage gives all of them room.
screen: `3,306: ONLY THEIR POWERS.` · `33: VASUS, RUDRAS, ADITYAS, TWO MORE.` · `FOOD AND BREATH; THE WIND; THEN BREATH.` · `EKAM SAD VIPRA BAHUDHA VADANTI.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Start wide: notice everything you can hear and feel at once, the many. Then narrow to three things, then two, the air coming in and the body receiving it, then one and a half, the breath moving, then one: just breath. When the many come back, and they will, count down again, gently.
Vidagdha Shakalya. The challenger whose questions counted the gods down to ekam, one: breath, Brahman, That.
Your line: one. Tomorrow, Shakalya keeps on asking, and it costs him dearly. Rest well.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions hold many forms of the divine together with the conviction that the divine is one; ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti from the Rig Veda is often quoted for that idea, and the thirty-three gods are named in Vedic ritual.

pairs: the ten breaths and the self

it keeps them, and shows them folding down to one.

fork.setup: Shakalya asks: how many gods are there, really? you're Yajnavalkya, and you've already said 3,306. what's your next answer?
fork.reveal: thirty-three, and then six, three, two, one and a half, and one. each step folds the last one in, and keeps it.

original.note: Sanskrit ekam: one. ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti, truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways (Rig Veda 1.164.46).

trapdoor: what you thought: Hindus believe in millions of gods.
what it means: in this count, the many gods are real, and they fold down, step by step, into one.
what a scholar hears: 3.9.1–9's count of 3,306 comes from a ritual formula; the one and a half (adhyardha) is a pun on the wind in which all grows (adhyārdhnot).

chat.says: Isn't it a contradiction to honor many gods and say God is one?
options: In this text the many fold down to one, like a fan; none are thrown away.
Shakalya proves that one and a half is the true and final count of gods.
Yajnavalkya refuses to give any number, so the question stays open.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya counts 3,306 down to one, breath, Brahman, without calling the many a mistake: truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways.

Rudras.meaning: eleven: the ten breaths and the self, who make people weep

notes: The first number (3.9.1) is given as 'three and three hundred, three and three thousand' (303 + 3,003 = 3,306), drawn from the nivid of the hymn to the All-gods. Confirm.
Explanations of the Vasus (vas, dwell), Rudras (rud, weep), Adityas (carry along) follow the text's own wordplay (3.9.3–5); confirm.
The 'one' is identified as breath (prāṇa), Brahman, called tyad (3.9.9). Confirm.
'330 million gods' (tetis koti): koti can mean 'kind/type' or 'ten million'; this is a common explanation but debated. Confirm wording.
The three ways Hindus hold many and one are stated without ranking; confirm.
